title: Early Warning Indicators and Signs of Distress
summary: The quantitative and behavioural signals that typically precede firm distress, and how supervisors build them into monitoring so problems are spotted while there is still time to act.
contentGaps: Written as part of a programme: Aim and Purpose is the module's one-line description; audience, prior knowledge and core reading come from the programme

sections.Aim and Purpose: The quantitative and behavioural signals that typically precede firm distress, and how supervisors build them into monitoring so problems are spotted while there is still time to act.
Learning Objectives: Identify common early warning indicators across risk types
Distinguish behavioural from quantitative warning signs
Assess whether monitoring arrangements would detect distress in time
Syllabus: Capital, liquidity, earnings and funding indicators
Behavioural signals: management turnover, evasiveness and delayed reporting
Early warning dashboards and their limits
Intended Audience: Supervisors and risk specialists responsible for firms that may come under stress
Resolution, financial stability and macroprudential staff
Senior managers and executives who would lead or take decisions in the authority's crisis response
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of supervision, financial stability or risk work is helpful. No prior crisis or resolution experience is required.
Core Reading: FSB, Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions (2014)
Basel Committee, Guidelines for Identifying and Dealing with Weak Banks (2015)
IADI, Core Principles for Effective Deposit Insurance Systems
